result.title: AI-Generated Image Detectors Overrely on Global Artifacts: Evidence from Inpainting Exchange
result.venue_year: arXiv preprint (cs.CV; cs.AI), submitted 30 Jan 2026; no conference/journal venue listed in Comments (preprint only). Authors: Elif Nebioglu, Emirhan Bilgic, Adrian Popescu.
exact_claims: Hive Moderation (commercial API): 91.4% (standard INP) -> 54.8% (INP-X) — matches claim exactly
Sightengine (commercial API): 92.6% (INP) -> 55.0% (INP-X) — matches claim exactly
Corvi2023 (academic detector): 94.2% (INP) -> 55.4% (INP-X) — matches claim exactly
SPAI (academic detector): 66.1% (INP) -> 54.2% (INP-X) — matches claim exactly
Additional detector found: DNF 71.0% (INP) -> 60.4% (INP-X)
Abstract summary phrasing: detectors drop 'from 91% to 55%, frequently approaching chance level'
Dataset: 90K-image benchmark, 30k samples each for 3 subsets (real / standard inpainted / exchanged inpainted), built over four source datasets: CelebA-HQ, CityScapes, OpenImages, SUN-RGBD
Mechanism claim: failures attributed to VAE-based reconstruction inducing a pervasive spectral shift across the whole image including unedited regions
Mask size finding: increasing mask size generally correlates with higher detection accuracy (no explicit numeric size x blending sweep quoted)
Comments field: 21 pages, 15 figures, 6 tables
Code/data: https://github.com/emirhanbilgic/INP-X
result.what_they_did: Introduced Inpainting Exchange (INP-X), an operation that keeps the AI-synthesized inpainted region but restores the original real pixels everywhere outside the mask, then re-evaluated pretrained state-of-the-art AI-image detectors (academic + commercial APIs) on a 90K-image benchmark. They show that this collapses detector accuracy to near chance (e.g. Hive 91.4->54.8, Sightengine 92.6->55.0, Corvi2023 94.2->55.4, SPAI 66.1->54.2), arguing detectors over-rely on global VAE-induced spectral artifacts rather than the locally synthesized content, and propose content-aware detection.
result.what_they_did_NOT_do: No fraud-domain focus whatsoever: no fabricated insurance / auto / property / hotel damage and no receipts. Source datasets are faces and scenes (CelebA-HQ, CityScapes, OpenImages, SUN-RGBD), not fraud documents. They do not run a systematic mask-size x blending-strength sweep with quoted numbers (only a qualitative 'larger mask -> higher accuracy' trend). Commercial APIs are limited to Hive and Sightengine; no broader commercial-API panel. No laundering / re-compression / social-media re-upload robustness pipeline is evaluated. The defensive 'small localized edit on an authentic photo for fraud' framing is the verifier's project context, not the paper's stated motivation.
result.confidence: high — id, title, authors, submission date, and all four claimed collapse numbers (Hive 91.4->54.8, Sightengine 92.6->55.0, Corvi2023 94.2->55.4, SPAI 66.1->54.2) independently confirmed across the arXiv abs page, arXiv HTML full text, HuggingFace papers page, and web search. Only the venue (preprint, no conference) and the absence of any fraud-domain content are clarifications, not discrepancies.

result.title: Detecting Localized Deepfakes: How Well Do Synthetic Image Detectors Handle Inpainting?
result.venue_year: arXiv preprint (2512 = Dec 2025), v1; no conference/journal venue stated. Authors: Serafino Pandolfini, Lorenzo Pellegrini, Matteo Ferrara, Davide Maltoni (University of Bologna, Italy)
exact_claims: <5% mask area: 'all detectors perform near chance' (qualitative, matches the claimed '<5% mask area approx chance')
>20% mask area: 'performance improves substantially' (qualitative, matches the claimed 'recovery >20%')
DINOv3 reaches performance comparable to fully-generated-image detection at ~65% mask size
DINOv2 requires >80% mask size to reach comparable performance
Detectors evaluated as main backbones: ResNet-50 CLIP, DINOv2 ViT-L/14, DINOv3 ViT-L/16; DINOv3 > DINOv2 > ResNet-50
Comparison/baseline methods: CNNDetect, DIMD, Dire, FreqDetect, UnivFD, Fusing, GramNet, LGrad, NPR, RINE, DeFake, PatchCraft
Datasets: BR-Gen (150,000 inpainted / 15,000 real), TGIF (74,808 inpainted / 9,372 real), TGIF2 (112,464 inpainted / 6,248 real); real images from COCO2017, ImageNet, Places

Headline AUROC examples: BR-Gen DINOv3 = 0.86; TGIF fully-regenerated uncompressed DINOv3 = 0.96 (SD2) / 0.92 (SDXL); TGIF2 DINOv3 = 0.52 (NOTE: these specific AUROC values came from the fast-model extraction and could not be independently re-confirmed against a table in the HTML; treat the 0.86/0.96/0.92/0.52 figures as lower-confidence)
result.what_they_did: Systematically evaluated synthetic-image (deepfake) detectors that were originally trained on fully synthetic images, testing how well they transfer to localized inpainting / region-level edits. They analyze detection AUROC as a function of mask size (percentage of image area modified) across three inpainting datasets (BR-Gen, TGIF, TGIF2) using ResNet-50 CLIP, DINOv2 ViT-L/14, and DINOv3 ViT-L/16 backbones plus many prior detectors as baselines. Core finding: detectors rely on global artifacts, so very small edits (<5% area) are near chance, performance recovers as mask grows past ~20%, and large masks (~65% for DINOv3, >80% for DINOv2) approach fully-synthetic-image performance.
result.what_they_did_NOT_do: The paper has NO fraud-domain focus whatsoever — no mention of insurance, auto/property/hotel damage, receipts, or any fraud/claims application. It is a general inpainting-detection benchmark on natural-image datasets (COCO/ImageNet/Places real images). It does NOT report a size x JPEG/blending sweep in the fraud sense (it does note compression effects, e.g. 'uncompressed' TGIF results, but not a deliberate laundering/blending robustness study), does NOT test commercial detection APIs (only open academic backbones/methods), and does NOT study laundering/anti-forensic post-processing as an adversarial dimension. Note also: the '<5% ≈ chance' and '>20% recovery' claims are stated QUALITATIVELY in the text/Figure 4, not as a clean per-bin numeric table; discrete bins (0-5%, 5-10%, etc.) are not formally defined.
result.confidence: High that the paper exists with this exact ID, title, authors, the three datasets (BR-Gen/TGIF/TGIF2), the three main detector backbones (ResNet-50 CLIP / DINOv2 / DINOv3), and the qualitative <5%-chance and >20%-recovery + 65%/80% mask claims. Medium-low on the specific per-dataset AUROC point values (0.86/0.96/0.92/0.52) and dataset image counts, which came from a fast-model HTML extraction and were not cross-confirmed against a rendered table. Confirmed: NO fraud/insurance/receipt domain content.

result.paper: AIForge-Doc: A Benchmark for Detecting AI-Forged Tampering in Financial and Form Documents (arXiv:2602.20569)
result.title: AIForge-Doc: A Benchmark for Detecting AI-Forged Tampering in Financial and Form Documents
result.venue_year: arXiv preprint, submitted 24 Feb 2026 (v1); no peer-reviewed venue confirmed
exact_claims: Median tampered area = 0.92% of total image pixels (IQR [0.35%, 1.55%]); >99% of pixels unmodified per image. This matches the claimed '~1% median-area' (the precise figure is 0.92%, not exactly 1%).
DocTamper AUC collapses 0.98 (own in-distribution test set) -> 0.563 [0.535, 0.591] on AIForge-Doc — exactly matches the claimed 0.98->0.563 collapse.
TruFor AUC = 0.751 [0.726, 0.776] zero-shot/OOD vs 0.96 on NIST16 reference.
GPT-4o zero-shot judge AUC = 0.509 [0.481, 0.537] — essentially chance/random baseline.
Pixel-level: DocTamper IoU = 0.020 (F1 0.030); TruFor IoU = 0.358 (F1 0.434), pixel-AUC 0.916; DocTamper pixel-AUC 0.675.

Dataset = 4,061 forged images (3,249 train / 812 test, 80/20 split) from 4 public document datasets: CORD (1,000), WildReceipt (1,696), SROIE (946), XFUND (419), across 9 languages, DocTamper-compatible pixel-precise masks.
AI inpainting APIs: Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (89.6%) and Ideogram v2 Edit (10.4%).
Authors: Jiaqi Wu, Yuchen Zhou, Muduo Xu, Zisheng Liang, Simiao Ren, Jiayu Xue, Meige Yang, Siying Chen, Jingheng Huan.
result.what_they_did: Built the first benchmark targeting diffusion/AI-inpainting-based localized tampering of numeric fields in real financial and form documents (receipts/forms). Used two commercial inpainting APIs (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, Ideogram v2 Edit) to forge numeric fields on 4,061 real document images from CORD/WildReceipt/SROIE/XFUND, with pixel-precise tampered-region masks. Benchmarked three representative detectors zero-shot (TruFor, DocTamper, GPT-4o judge) and showed all degrade sharply vs their reference/in-distribution performance, with DocTamper's image-level AUC collapsing from 0.98 to 0.563 and near-zero pixel IoU (0.020), GPT-4o at chance (0.509). Concludes existing forgery detectors (trained on Photoshop/GIMP-style edits) are blind to AI-forged document tampering.
result.what_they_did_NOT_do: Scope is strictly DOCUMENT/receipt/form images — it does NOT touch the insurance/auto/property/hotel damage-photo fraud domain or any natural-scene authentic photos. Edits are limited to localized numeric-field forgery; excludes wholesale document synthesis and signature forgery. Does NOT run a systematic size x blending sweep (it reports the area distribution but does not vary mask size/blend as an experimental axis). Does NOT evaluate commercial detector APIs (only TruFor, DocTamper, and a GPT-4o zero-shot judge). Does NOT test laundering / post-processing robustness (JPEG recompression, resize, screenshot, print-scan, etc.). So it is a strong fraud-domain analogue for the 'small localized AI edit collapses detectors' thesis, but on documents only, without the damage-photo domain, the size/blend sweep, commercial APIs, or laundering robustness.
result.confidence: high — confirmed via both the arXiv abstract page and the arXiv HTML full text (arxiv.org/html/2602.20569v1); cross-checked numbers, also indexed on ResearchGate and covered by trade press (Eftsure, ChannelNews). The only discrepancy is cosmetic: median area is 0.92%, described as '~1%' in the claim.

key_works.oneline: Shows SOTA AI-image detectors flag inpainted images via image-wide (VAE spectral-shift) artifacts, not the actually-synthesized local region.
key_works.key_result: Their Inpainting-Exchange intervention (restore real pixels outside the edit, keep synthesized content) drops SOTA and commercial detectors from ~91% to ~55% accuracy (near chance); 90K test set of real/inpainted/exchanged images.

key_works.title: Detecting Localized Deepfakes: How Well Do Synthetic Image Detectors Handle Inpainting?
key_works.venue: arXiv preprint (2512.16688); Pandolfini, Pellegrini, Ferrara, Maltoni (Univ. Bologna)
key_works.oneline: Benchmarks whether detectors trained on fully-synthetic images transfer to localized inpainting edits as the edited region shrinks.
key_works.key_result: Detectors are near random on edits <5% of image area; usable only above ~20% mask coverage. Best model (DINOv3 ViT-L) ~0.86 AUROC on large-mask BR-Gen but ~0.52 (chance) on Flux-based small-edit TGIF2. key_works.title: The Unwinnable Arms Race of AI Image Detection
key_works.venue: arXiv preprint (2509.21135); Aczel, Vettor, Plesner, Wattenhofer (ETH Zurich)
key_works.oneline: Argues detection faces a structural asymmetry: generators improve faster than detectors generalize.
key_works.key_result: Detectors trained on one generator degrade sharply on newer generators; simple post-processing (compression, resize, noise) substantially lowers accuracy, undermining real-world deployment — i.e., retraining cannot indefinitely keep pace.

key_works.title: Methods and Trends in Detecting AI-Generated Images: A Comprehensive Review
key_works.oneline: Taxonomy of 7 detection families (spatial CNN, frequency, fingerprint, patch, training-free reconstruction, CLIP/VLM, MLLM) with cross-generator/cross-scene robustness analysis.
key_works.key_result: Spatial CNN detectors generalize poorly cross-generator; CLIP/VLM and training-free reconstruction methods (AEROBLADE, RIGID) generalize best. Lists standard benchmarks (GenImage, UnivFD, DiffusionForensics, SynthBuster, CIFAKE); notes most methods do binary classification, not manipulation localization.

key_works.title: Verifying Provenance of Digital Media: Why the C2PA Specifications Fall Short
key_works.venue: arXiv preprint (2604.24890); Golaszewski, Krawetz, Sherman et al.
key_works.oneline: Security analysis of C2PA Content Credentials as a media-authenticity mechanism.
key_works.key_result: Six failure modes: uncryptographically-bound timestamps, broken certificate-revocation checking (a revoked Nikon cert still validated months later), inconsistent validators (same image valid in one tool, invalid in another), exclusion-range gaps (GPS editable undetected), cert expiry within months, and self-reported conformance. Crucially: absence of credentials is NOT evidence of fraud, and cameras can sign AI images.

key_works.title: Fighting Fake News: Image Splice Detection via Learned Self-Consistency (EXIF-as-supervision)
key_works.venue: ECCV 2018; Huh, Liu, Owens, Efros (UC Berkeley)
key_works.oneline: Foundational method: train a model to predict EXIF self-consistency so spliced regions (different imaging pipelines) light up — the conceptual basis of metadata/PRNU-style forensics now used commercially.
key_works.key_result: Detects and localizes splices without manipulation labels by exploiting that composited regions come from different capture pipelines; underpins the 'multiple noise-pattern = manipulation' logic vendors like Verisk describe.

result.what_detection_runs_today: In production claims pipelines the dominant, reliable checks are classical and database-driven, not AI-vs-AI: (1) perceptual-hash / image-similarity DEDUP of a submitted photo against the insurer's and the industry-shared database (Verisk ClaimSearch dedup, FRISS reused-media, Shift similarity scoring) — this is the single most effective real defense and catches photo reuse/recycling regardless of how the image was made; (2) EXIF/metadata consistency (capture timestamp vs incident date, GPS vs loss location, device/make-model, web-download/processing software traces) — cheap and widely used but trivially spoofable/strippable, so it is treated as a soft signal; (3) reverse-image / internet-source search to catch photos scraped from the web; (4) noise-pattern/PRNU and pixel-level splice forensics (a single image containing more than one camera noise signature implies compositing) — Verisk and FRISS describe this for copy-move/splice; (5) document/PDF tamper checks and OCR-based receipt/invoice validation (math, tax, merchant existence, generator fingerprints) for fabricated receipts/estimates; (6) graph/network analytics linking claims via shared intermediaries, devices, IPs; (7) capture-side defenses (VAARHAFT SafeCam, Tractable live-guided capture) that lock the camera and detect screen re-photography to stop replay/screenshot spoofing. Dedicated AI-GENERATED-image detectors are the newest and least mature layer: Verisk's GenAI detection was described as beta/in-development, VAARHAFT/SAS market full-synthetic-image detection, but published, independently-verified accuracy on small localized edits is essentially absent. C2PA provenance is discussed (Guidewire) and increasingly camera-supported (Pixel 10, Samsung AI-edit tagging) but not yet a load-bearing claims check.
result.the_gap: The defensive thesis is well-supported by current evidence: deployed pipelines are strongest against photo REUSE (hashing/dedup) and crude splices (noise-pattern), and weakest against small localized AI inpainting on an otherwise-authentic photo. Three forces converge. (a) Academic results show off-the-shelf and even commercial AI-image detectors collapse to near-chance on small edits: near-random below ~5% mask area, only usable above ~20% coverage (Pandolfini et al. 2025), and a 91%->55% drop when detectors are denied the global VAE artifact and forced to judge the actually-synthesized region (Nebioglu et al. 2026). A fabricated dent/scratch/water-stain is exactly such a small local edit. (b) Metadata/EXIF defenses fail by construction here because the base photo is a genuine capture with a genuine camera/timestamp/GPS — only a small region is altered, so metadata stays consistent. (c) Hash/dedup fails because the image is novel (not reused), and noise-pattern forensics is increasingly defeated by modern diffusion inpainting that re-harmonizes noise. C2PA does not close the gap: absence of credentials is uninformative, cameras can sign AI content, and revocation/validation are broken (Golaszewski et al. 2026); and even where a phone signs originals, an inpainted-then-recaptured image can carry a fresh valid signature. Vendors themselves disclaim completeness (VAARHAFT 'never 100%', FRISS 'not a complete solution', SAS survey: only 7% of anti-fraud pros feel more than moderately prepared). Net: the small-localized-edit-on-authentic-photo threat is the documented blind spot, and a stress-test benchmark in the insurance-damage domain (which does not publicly exist) is the clear unmet need.
fraud_scale_facts: Insurance fraud costs US consumers an estimated $308.6 billion/year; roughly 1 in 10 property-casualty losses includes fraud (SAS / Coalition Against Insurance Fraud, 2026).
Non-health insurance fraud is estimated at >$40 billion/year in the US (Coalition Against Insurance Fraud, cited by SimpleSolve/FRISS).
Shift Technology estimate (widely re-cited by Guidewire, SimpleSolve): 20-30% of insurance claims may now include some form of altered images, fabricated documents, or synthetic media.
Only 7% of anti-fraud professionals say their organization is more than moderately prepared for AI-driven fraud, and no insurance respondents exceeded 'moderate' (ACFE + SAS survey, 2026).

Verisk ClaimSearch scale: >95% of the industry contributes images, 315 insurers signed up to contribute; a 768,000-image study found 1,967 duplicates, one photo reused across 44 claims, with duplicates tied to ~$5.3M indemnity across 1,475 claims (Verisk / Reinsurance News, 2023).

Receipt fraud: AI-generated receipts were ~14% of fraudulent documents submitted in September 2025 vs ~0% a year earlier (AppZen, via Ars Technica/FT); surge attributed to OpenAI's March 2025 GPT-4o image generation. 3.5M+ fake receipts created on the top four fake-receipt sites in six months (AppZen).
Deloitte 2025: 35% of insurance executives rank fraud detection among their top GenAI priorities (cited by Guidewire).

Illustrative deployed catches/losses: an $85K homeowners claim approved on deepfake video before a post-payout audit (SimpleSolve); a NL claimant collected ~€150k on AI-forged medical records before being caught; an Airbnb host used manipulated damage photos for a £12k claim (FRISS).
result.ethics_data_notes: This is a defensive stress-test program; outputs must not become an evasion playbook. Concrete guardrails grounded in the sources: (1) Do not publish or operationalize specific recipes for defeating named vendors (e.g., exact mask sizes, generators, or recapture tricks that evade Verisk/FRISS/VAARHAFT) — report capability gaps at the level of detector families and threat classes, as the academic papers do. (2) Build evaluation data ethically: use public forgery/inpainting benchmarks (GenImage, DiffusionForensics, BR-Gen/TGIF, INP-X, AutoSplice/CocoGlide) and synthetically-edited photos you generate or license; do NOT scrape real insurer claim images (PII, GDPR — note ClaimSearch-class corpora are proprietary and access-controlled). VAARHAFT explicitly markets GDPR-aligned handling and on-device hashing, signalling the privacy bar. (3) Real claim photos contain PII (faces, plates, addresses, geolocation) and health data in some lines — minimize, anonymize, and avoid retaining EXIF/GPS. (4) Coordinated disclosure: findings about a specific deployed detector's blind spot should go to the vendor/insurer before any public release. (5) Be precise that fabricating insurance claims is a crime; framing must stay strictly red-team/defense. (6) Watermark/label all AI-edited test images as synthetic to prevent leakage into real claims or training sets.

The trustworthy quantitative robustness numbers here come from academic papers (91%->55%; <5% mask = near chance), not vendors.","Some cited stats are circular/second-hand: the '20-30% of claims include altered media' figure traces to a single Shift Technology estimate re-quoted across many blogs; the $308.6B and $40B fraud figures are industry/advocacy estimates with broad methodology.","I could not fully load several primary vendor product pages (Verisk Digital Media Forensics and the Verisk/Guidewire blogs were JS-rendered, returning only titles on direct fetch); Verisk technical details (noise-pattern, dedup, GenAI-beta) were reconstructed from search snippets + the 2023 Reinsurance News piece, so exact current feature status (e.g., whether GenAI detection has exited beta in 2026) is uncertain.","Dates skew the picture: the Verisk 768K-image study and '315 insurers' figures are from 2023 and may now be larger; VAARHAFT pilot counts are from mid-2024.","No public insurance-damage-specific manipulation benchmark was found despite targeted searches; the small-localized-edit evidence comes from general-domain inpainting benchmarks (BR-Gen/TGIF/INP-X) used as proxies — domain transfer to car/property/hotel damage is plausible but unverified.","FRISS/Shift relationship to acquisitions/consolidation in the insurtech fraud space could not be confirmed; treat vendor org details as point-in-time.","Clearspeed and parts of Tractable/Duck Creek are adjacent (voice, estimation, distribution) rather than image-forensic engines; included for completeness of the claims-triage stack, not as image detectors.","C2PA adoption is moving fast (camera support in 2025-2026) but its value as a claims-fraud check remains weak per the 2026 shortcomings paper; any conclusion about C2PA should be revisited as spec v2.x and revocation handling mature."]

result.topic: Document / receipt / invoice forgery and tamper detection — the expense/medical/claims-document branch. Covers AI-inpainting robustness of academic detectors (DocTamper/DTD, AIForge-Doc, DocForge-Bench, Tampered-IC13/T-SROIE, ADCD-Net, TextSleuth) plus deployed expense-audit/document-verification products (AppZen, SAP Concur Verify/Detect, Ramp, Inscribe, Resistant AI).

key_works.title: AIForge-Doc: A Benchmark for Detecting AI-Forged Tampering in Financial and Form Documents
key_works.oneline: First benchmark that forges NUMERIC FIELDS of real receipts/forms exclusively with diffusion/AI inpainting APIs (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, Ideogram v2 Edit) and gives pixel masks; directly on-topic for stress-testing detectors against small localized AI edits of numbers.
key_works.key_result: 4,061 forged images from CORD/WildReceipt/SROIE/XFUND, 9 languages; median tampered area only 0.92% of pixels. Zero-shot detectors collapse: document-specific DocTamper drops to AUC 0.563 (vs 0.98 in-distribution) and IoU 0.020 (vs 0.71); general TruFor AUC 0.751 (vs 0.96 on NIST16); GPT-4o AUC 0.509 (random). 5 of 7 inpainting tools were rejected for failing to produce legible/correct-valued text.

key_works.title: DocForge-Bench: A Comprehensive 0-shot Benchmark for Document Forgery Detection and Analysis
key_works.oneline: Unified zero-shot benchmark of 14 detectors across 8 document-forgery datasets; diagnoses that the dominant failure is calibration/threshold, not just feature discrimination, and flags AIGC editing as the open gap.
key_works.key_result: No method reaches F1>=0.3 on 6+ datasets; Pixel-AUC>=0.76 for most methods yet Pixel-F1 ~0.02-0.35 because tampered pixels are only 0.27-4.17% of the image. Threshold adaptation on just N=10 in-domain images recovers 39-55% of the oracle-F1 gap. All 8 datasets predate generative-AI editing.

key_works.title: Towards Robust Tampered Text Detection in Document Image: New Dataset and New Solution (DocTamper / DTD)
key_works.oneline: Introduced DocTamper, the most-used document-tamper-localization dataset, and DTD, a JPEG/DCT frequency-aware detector trained with curriculum learning to resist compression — the de-facto baseline that AIForge-Doc/DocForge-Bench show fails on AI inpainting.
key_works.key_result: 170k images (120k train; test split Test 30k / FCD 2k / SCD 18k) over contracts, invoices, receipts, books; tampering = copy-move, splicing, print. DTD uses a Frequency Perception Head over DCT coefficients + curriculum learning (CLTD) to stay robust to JPEG; strong in-distribution but generalizes poorly to diffusion inpainting. Non-commercial, password-gated.

key_works.title: ADCD-Net: Robust Document Image Forgery Localization via Adaptive DCT Feature and Hierarchical Content Disentanglement
key_works.oneline: State-of-the-art document forgery localizer that adaptively fuses JPEG-DCT coefficients with RGB and OCR-derived character masks — illustrates why detectors over-rely on JPEG/compression artifacts that AI inpainting + re-photographing can wash out.
key_works.key_result: Combines adaptive DCT features, RGB stream, and OCR character masks with hierarchical content disentanglement for SOTA on document benchmarks; the DCT dependence is exactly the signal that screenshots/re-saves of AI receipts degrade.

key_works.title: TextSleuth: Towards Explainable Tampered Text Detection
key_works.oneline: MLLM/VLM-based detector that not only localizes tampered text but explains the anomaly in natural language; introduces the ETTD (Explainable Tampered Text Detection) dataset covering insertion/deletion/replacement.
key_works.key_result: Moves beyond binary masks to grounded explanations of why text looks manipulated; targets both traditional edits and AI/LLM-generated text. (Sibling line: GPT-4o used zero-shot in AIForge-Doc scored near-random AUC 0.509, showing off-the-shelf VLMs are not yet reliable localizers.)

key_works.title: Detecting Tampered Scene Text in the Wild (Tampered-IC13) and Generalized Tampered Scene Text Detection / OSTF
key_works.venue: ECCV 2022; AAAI 2025 (Wang et al. / Qu et al.)
key_works.oneline: Tampered-IC13 is the first word-level tampered-scene-text dataset (built on ICDAR2013, edited with SR-Net); OSTF extends it with forgeries from nine modern generative models, tracking the shift from one editor to many AI editors.
key_works.key_result: Tampered-IC13: ~300 scene-text images tampered by SR-Net, box-level labels (1=real text, 2=tampered). OSTF re-forges with 9 latest deep generative models, demonstrating that single-generator-trained detectors do not transfer across generators.

key_works.title: Find it again! — Receipt Dataset for Document Forgery Detection (and T-SROIE)
key_works.oneline: Realistic receipt-forgery datasets built on SROIE: 'Find it again!' modifies real scanned receipts; T-SROIE was the first to localize AIGC-style (SR-Net) tampering in scanned receipts — closest public analogues to fabricated expense receipts.
key_works.key_result: 'Find it again!' = 988 SROIE-derived scanned receipts, 163 with realistic fraudulent modifications. T-SROIE localizes SR-Net-style tampering on high-res uncropped receipts. Both predate diffusion-API inpainting.

result.what_detection_runs_today: Two largely separate stacks. (1) ACADEMIC localization: pixel-level tamper localizers that lean heavily on JPEG/DCT compression artifacts and text-region cues — DocTamper/DTD (Frequency Perception Head over DCT + curriculum learning to survive recompression), ADCD-Net (adaptive DCT + RGB + OCR character masks), CTP-Net (character-texture two-stream), ASCFormer/RealTextManipulation, plus general image-forensics nets (TruFor, CAT-Net, MVSS-Net, ManTraNet, PSCC-Net, IML-ViT, SAFIRE). Newer MLLM/VLM approaches (TextSleuth, TextShield-R1) add explanations. (2) DEPLOYED expense/claims verification: AppZen, SAP Concur Verify/Detect, Ramp, Inscribe, Resistant AI. In production these rely far more on METADATA and CROSS-REFERENCE signals than on pixel forensics: EXIF/PDF metadata and generator fingerprints, PDF revision history, font/kerning anomalies, mathematical consistency (line items/tax/totals), merchant-existence and inventory checks, duplicate/template-reuse detection, and cross-document corroboration (receipt vs card transaction, pay stub vs bank deposits). SAP Concur and Inscribe both add some image/generator-artifact analysis on top.
result.the_gap: Small, localized AI inpainting of numeric fields on otherwise-authentic photos is the documented blind spot. (1) Academic localizers trained on copy-move/splice/JPEG-composite collapse on diffusion inpainting: in AIForge-Doc the document-specialist DocTamper falls to AUC 0.563 / IoU 0.020 and general TruFor to AUC 0.751, while a zero-shot VLM (GPT-4o) is random (0.509). (2) The tampered area is tiny — median ~0.92% of pixels (0.27-4.17% across DocForge-Bench) — so even when ranking is okay (Pixel-AUC>=0.76) the fixed-threshold Pixel-F1 stays ~0.02-0.35; DocForge-Bench shows this is largely a CALIBRATION failure (adapting a threshold on just 10 in-domain images recovers 39-55% of the gap), not pure feature failure. (3) Deployed metadata defenses are brittle by their vendors' own admission: SAP Concur states that once an AI receipt is screenshotted or re-photographed the identifying metadata is erased, defeating metadata-based detection — exactly the 'edit a real photo' threat model. (4) Detectors over-fit to JPEG/DCT statistics that AI generation + re-photographing disrupt, and to specific generators (single-generator training does not transfer, per OSTF). Net: there is no public detector that reliably localizes small AI numeric-field edits on real claim/expense photos today, and benchmarks (AIForge-Doc, DocForge-Bench) postdate the threat by only months.

result.ethics_data_notes: All recommended datasets are real-photo-derived and either public-research or non-commercial. DocTamper is password-gated, non-commercial, education-email only. AIForge-Doc is released under CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (non-commercial, share-alike) and frames itself as defensive (closing a detector blind spot); the abstract/metadata viewed did not expose a full ethics statement, and it was not confirmed from the pages fetched whether the exact generation prompts/recipe are withheld — treat that as unverified (see caveats). Base receipt/form corpora (SROIE, CORD, WildReceipt, XFUND) are standard research OCR datasets containing real receipts/forms with PII-like fields (merchant, totals, addresses), so derived forgery sets inherit privacy considerations; use under their research licenses only. For a DEFENSIVE stress-test, prefer evaluating released detector weights on AIForge-Doc / DocForge-Bench / T-SROIE rather than regenerating new forged numeric fields; if generation is needed, keep it to localized synthetic numeric edits on already-public research images, never on third-party real claims, and do not publish generation recipes. This report intentionally contains no operational forgery/evasion recipe.
result.caveats: Uncertainty flags: (1) arXiv IDs 2602.20569 (AIForge-Doc) and 2603.01433 (DocForge-Bench) carry 2026 month-codes and Scam.ai/academic authorship; the headline numbers (DocTamper AUC 0.563 / IoU 0.020; Pixel-F1 0.02-0.35; 39-55% calibration recovery) come from those papers' own self-reported tables and were not independently reproduced — treat as authors' claims. (2) AIForge-Doc's exact license (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0) and whether it withholds generation prompts came from the arXiv abstract/metadata view, not the full PDF's ethics section, which I could not fully fetch (HTTP/size errors); verify in the PDF before relying on it. (3) Vendor statistics (AppZen 14% / 3.5M, Ramp $1M/90d, SAP Concur 18x / 80M, Inscribe $150k/5x/73%, Resistant AI 1-in-4 / 1-in-50, Medius 30%) are self-reported marketing figures with no independent audit and varying measurement windows — directional, not benchmark-grade. (4) Deployed products do not disclose model internals, so 'metadata/cross-reference vs pixel forensics' weighting is inferred from public pages. (5) DTD/ADCD-Net method specifics (Frequency Perception Head, curriculum learning, OCR masks) were partly drawn from search summaries because the CVPR PDF and ADCD-Net PDF failed to fetch (socket close / size limit); core claims are corroborated across multiple sources but exact figures should be checked in the papers. (6) GPT-4o zero-shot AUC 0.509 reflects naive prompting, not a tuned VLM pipeline. (7) Some sources are US-search-biased; non-US deployed tools may be underrepresented.

result.what_detection_runs_today: Production claim-photo screening combines: (1) metadata/EXIF forensics (timestamp vs. claimed-incident date, GPS, device, software tags, double-JPEG/quantization-table checks) as used by Zurich SIU; (2) computer-vision similarity/anomaly models that compare submitted damage against genuine damage and reverse-image-search for reused stock/salvage photos (Allianz); (3) commercial 'AI-generated/manipulated image detection' APIs (Inaza, TruthScan, SimpleSolve, plus Verisk analytics) — largely vendor-benchmarked; and (4) emerging provenance via C2PA/Content Credentials at capture. Academically, the relevant detectors are image-manipulation localization / inpainting-detection models trained/evaluated on IMD2020, CASIA, NIST16, COCO-Inpaint, and GIM. Key weakness the project targets: most of this is tuned to splicing, full AI-generation, or compression artifacts — small localized generative edits (inpainting) on otherwise authentic, re-encoded claim photos with stripped EXIF are the hardest and least-covered case.
result.the_gap: There is no public benchmark of authentic damage photos carrying small, localized, modern AI edits (inpaint/object-add/remove) at claim-realistic resolution and re-encoding. Existing damage datasets (CarDD, VehiDE, xBD, MVTec) are real bases but were built for damage *detection*, not edit-provenance, and most are sourced from Flickr/Shutterstock/satellite/studio — so they usually lack original consumer-camera EXIF (the very metadata insurers rely on). Existing manipulation benchmarks (IMD2020, CASIA, COCO-Inpaint, GIM) use generic non-damage content and often older edit styles. So the project must marry a real damage base (CarDD/VehiDE/Roboflow auto sets; SROIE/CORD receipts; small furniture sets) with controlled localized AI edits, and decide whether to (a) accept EXIF-stripped bases or (b) re-capture / use provenance-bearing bases (SIDD/RAISE/Forchheim style) to study the metadata-forensics axis. No public hotel-room damage dataset of meaningful scale currently exists — a genuine collection gap.

result.ethics_data_notes: Defensive framing only: this maps authentic bases for a controlled detector stress-test; no operational fraud/evasion method is provided. Data/licensing constraints to respect: CarDD requires a signed license and is bound by Flickr/Shutterstock terms (non-commercial, no redistribution of source images); xBD is CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 (non-commercial, share-alike); MVTec AD is non-commercial research only; many Kaggle/Roboflow damage sets are community-scraped with unclear or absent licenses and possible third-party copyright — verify each before use and avoid redistributing base images. Receipts (CORD/SROIE) and any real claim photos can contain PII (names, addresses, license plates, prices, GPS in EXIF); CORD already withholds 10k images for that reason — scrub/redact and avoid re-identifiable content. If building an edited-image benchmark, label every edited sample clearly as synthetic, restrict to research distribution, and prefer provenance/consent-clean bases where possible. Editing real people's property photos raises consent issues even for defensive research.
result.caveats: Several headline fraud numbers are vendor/press-sourced (Verisk, SAS, Admiral, insurtech vendors) and not independently audited; the $308.6B is total US fraud (Coalition Against Insurance Fraud), NOT AI-edit-specific — treat the 23%/42%/55%/40-50% figures as directional. The Verisk 2026 PDF would not parse as text, so its exact numbers come from secondary reporting (PRNewswire, ROI-NJ, ECIKS) and may differ slightly from the primary release. EXIF/provenance claims are inferred: CarDD draws on Flickr/Shutterstock which routinely strip EXIF, and xBD/MVTec are satellite/studio, so 'no real consumer-camera provenance' is a strong inference, not a per-image audit — verify by sampling actual files. VehiDE's exact Kaggle license, file size, and format were not confirmed (page would not render); check the live Kaggle page. Roboflow/Kaggle image counts and licenses drift over time. No sizeable public hotel-room/furniture damage dataset was found (only tiny Roboflow sets and a hosted Nyckel classifier) — this is a likely real gap rather than a search miss, but worth a deeper targeted search before concluding. Dataset availability and download mechanisms (forms, registrations) can change; reconfirm access at build time.

result.topic: Tampered / AI-generated photo evidence in insurance fraud and courts: documented scale of doctored-photo claim fraud, legal-forensic evidentiary standards for AI-edited/deepfake evidence, and the academic forensics literature on authenticating tampered images — used to motivate defensive stress-testing of AI-image detectors against small, localized AI edits on otherwise-authentic damage/receipt photos.

key_works.title: Can VLMs Detect and Localize Fine-Grained AI-Edited Images? (FragFake benchmark)
key_works.venue: arXiv preprint (Sun, Zhang, Luo, et al.)
key_works.oneline: Builds FragFake, a large-scale benchmark of diffusion-edited images across source datasets, editors, and edit types, and frames detection+localization (not just binary) as a VLM task.
key_works.key_result: Pretrained VLMs incl. GPT-4o perform poorly at detecting/localizing localized edits; fine-tuned models (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL) reach high accuracy and much higher object precision — i.e., off-the-shelf detectors fail on fine-grained edits, the exact threat model of this project.

key_works.title: COCO-Inpaint: A Benchmark for Detecting and Localizing Inpainting-Based Image Manipulations
key_works.venue: arXiv preprint (Yan, Hong, Zhan, et al.)
key_works.oneline: Benchmark of 238,302 inpainted images from six SOTA inpainting models, four mask strategies, optional text guidance, targeting intrinsic real-vs-inpainted inconsistencies rather than semantic artifacts.
key_works.key_result: Provides a rigorous protocol exposing that existing image-manipulation-detection-and-localization (IMDL) methods struggle to generalize across inpainting generators — directly relevant to localized 'add/remove damage' edits.

key_works.title: TruFor: Leveraging all-round clues for trustworthy image forgery detection and localization
key_works.oneline: Fuses RGB with a learned noise-sensitive fingerprint (Noiseprint++) to produce a forgery localization map plus a confidence map and image-level integrity score.
key_works.key_result: Strong, widely-cited baseline for splicing/copy-move/inpainting localization on classic benchmarks; a standard detector to stress-test, but trained largely on non-diffusion forgeries so transfer to modern AI edits is a known weak point.

key_works.title: CAT-Net: Compression Artifact Tracing Network
key_works.oneline: First to feed JPEG DCT coefficients directly into a segmentation network and to jointly use RGB+DCT streams for forgery localization; trained on ~900k images.
key_works.key_result: Highest robustness across JPEG quality factors among contemporaries — a key baseline because real claim photos are re-compressed/messenger-laundered, which degrades most detectors.

key_works.title: DocTamper: Towards Robust Tampered Text Detection in Document Images
key_works.oneline: Large synthetic document-tampering dataset (120k train fakes; test splits DocTamper-Test 30k, FCD 2k, SCD 18k) over contracts, receipts, invoices, books with copy-move/splice/print edits, plus a robust detector.
key_works.key_result: Most widely used benchmark for receipt/invoice tampering localization — directly applicable to the fabricated-receipts arm of this project.

key_works.title: AIForge-Doc: A Benchmark for Detecting AI-Forged Tampering in Financial and Form Documents
key_works.oneline: First benchmark targeting diffusion-inpainting tampering specifically in financial/form documents (CORD, WildReceipt, SROIE, XFUND) across nine languages.
key_works.key_result: 4,061 forged document images isolating the modern AI-inpainting threat to receipts/invoices, where older copy-move/splice detectors underperform.

key_works.title: X-Edit: Detecting and Localizing Edits in Images Altered by Text-Guided Diffusion Models
key_works.oneline: Inverts an image with a pretrained diffusion model and feeds the inverted features to a segmentation network with channel/spatial attention to localize text-guided diffusion edits.
key_works.key_result: Demonstrates that diffusion-inversion features localize subtle text-guided edits better than RGB-only forensics — a SOTA candidate detector for the project's edit type.

key_works.title: AutoSplice: A Text-prompt Manipulated Image Dataset for Media Forensics
key_works.oneline: 3,621 manipulated + 2,273 authentic images created with language-guided (DALL-E 2-era) manipulation, one of the first text-prompt splicing forensics datasets.
key_works.key_result: Early evidence that diffusion/text-guided splices defeat detectors tuned on classic copy-move/splice corpora.

key_works.title: ForensicHub: A Unified Benchmark & Codebase for All-Domain Fake Image Detection and Localization
key_works.oneline: Unifies datasets, detectors, and evaluation across natural-image forgery, document tampering, deepfake, and AIGC detection domains.
key_works.key_result: Useful infrastructure to evaluate many baselines consistently against a common localized-edit threat model.

key_works.title: Deepfakes on trial / Adapting the Rules of Evidence for the Age of AI (legal-forensic analyses)
key_works.venue: Thomson Reuters Institute; Quinn Emanuel; ISBA; U. Baltimore Law Review
key_works.oneline: Surveys how courts authenticate AI/deepfake evidence under FRE 901/902/104, the proposed Rule 707 / draft Rule 901(c), and the 'liar's dividend'.
key_works.key_result: Documents that the current authentication bar is low (reasonable-jury, more-likely-than-not) and not designed for deepfakes, motivating better forensic tooling and provenance — the responsible-disclosure framing.

result.what_detection_runs_today: In claims practice, the dominant deployed defenses are NOT pixel-level AI-edit forensics but (1) image-similarity / duplicate detection to catch reused or recycled photos (Shift Technology), (2) metadata/EXIF and visual-consistency heuristics plus damage-pattern physics checks (Zurich, SAS red-flags: shadow angles, non-physical damage, blurred plates, too-clean backgrounds), (3) anomaly/network analytics and risk scoring on claim data, and (4) non-image triage like voice analytics (Clearspeed). Provenance via C2PA/Content Credentials is emerging but is opt-in, easily stripped, and only proves a manifest is untampered — it cannot certify an un-credentialed photo is authentic. In the forensics research stack, deployed/evaluated detectors are RGB+noise fusion models (TruFor, MMFusion/Noiseprint++), JPEG/DCT-aware models (CAT-Net), document-tamper localizers (DocTamper), and newer diffusion-edit localizers (X-Edit) and VLM-based detectors; per Verisk (Mar 2026), 65% of insurers use third-party AI detection tools and 50% use internally built ones, yet only 58% are 'very confident' detecting edits to real photos, 43% at scale, and 32% at spotting deepfakes — and 66% think most digital-media fraud goes undetected.
result.the_gap: The threat this project targets — small, localized AI edits (add a crack/dent, erase pre-existing damage, alter a receipt total) on an otherwise authentic photo — sits in the worst-case blind spot of current tooling. (1) Most fielded checks are similarity/metadata/physics heuristics that a fresh, single-source localized edit on a genuine photo can pass: it is not a duplicate, retains plausible EXIF, and only one small region is changed. (2) Academic detectors generalize poorly across unseen editors (GAN vs diffusion gap is large), degrade under JPEG/messenger re-compression, and the literature explicitly notes that when forensic artifacts are subtle, models fall back on semantic priors and miss faint manipulation cues; localization on small/non-object regions is the hardest case. (3) FragFake shows pretrained VLMs (incl. GPT-4o) are poor at fine-grained edit detection/localization, so 'just ask a foundation model' is not a reliable defense. (4) On the legal side, authentication standards (FRE 901, more-likely-than-not, reasonable-jury) were not built for deepfakes; proposed Rule 707/draft 901(c) mainly cover acknowledged-AI evidence, leaving disputed-authenticity edits under-addressed, and the 'liar's dividend' lets genuine photos be dismissed as fakes. The defensive contribution is a rigorous, edit-size-graded stress test of these detectors on realistic insurance/auto/property/hotel damage and receipt photos to quantify exactly where small localized edits evade detection — without publishing any edit/evasion recipe.

result.ethics_data_notes: This is defensive/measurement work: the goal is to quantify detector blind spots on small localized edits, not to produce manipulations. Recommended practices: (1) Use only authentic base photos with clear rights/consent or licensed/public datasets; for receipts/forms use de-identified or synthetic-PII versions of SROIE/CORD/WildReceipt/XFUND rather than real personal financial data. (2) Treat any generated tampered images as restricted research artifacts — do NOT release the edited images, masks-as-templates, prompt recipes, or per-editor evasion parameters; release only aggregate detector-performance metrics and, if needed, gated access under agreement. (3) Avoid real claimants' or real victims' damage photos scraped from social media (the exact fraud vector); synthesize or commission base imagery instead. (4) Coordinate responsible disclosure with detector vendors/insurers (Verisk, Shift, etc.) before publication, mirroring security-research norms. (5) Keep evaluation reproducible via public base datasets (DEFACTO, COCO-Inpaint, AutoSplice, IMD2020, DocTamper, AIForge-Doc) so others can verify findings without the withheld attack details. Legal-forensic framing (FRE 901/707, Mendones, liar's dividend) supports the public-interest justification: better-characterized detectors and provenance help courts and insurers, while careful artifact handling prevents misuse.
result.caveats: ["Several headline scale figures are insurer/vendor self-reported (Allianz, Zurich, Verisk, SAS/Adyen) and not independently audited; the widely-cited '300%' is a year-over-year rise off an unstated, likely small base and conflates 'shallowfakes' (Photoshop/app edits) with genuine AI/diffusion edits.","Verisk's March 2026 study is a survey (1,000 consumers + 300 professionals), so 'willingness/awareness' percentages reflect stated attitudes, not measured fraud rates; sampling/weighting details beyond US-only were not fully verified.","ABI/Allianz figures are UK-centric (£, UK market); US/other-market scale for AI-edited claim photos specifically is thinner and mostly anecdotal.","I could not load the Swiss Re SONAR 2025 page (HTTP 403) or the Verisk vendor page body directly; Verisk numbers came from the GlobeNewswire press release and trade coverage — treat exact percentages as press-release-sourced.","Several academic items are arXiv preprints (FragFake, COCO-Inpaint, AIForge-Doc, ManipShield, ForensicHub), some dated 2026, which may be non-peer-reviewed or pre-publication; benchmark counts and SOTA claims should be re-checked against final versions.","Some retrieved arXiv IDs carry future-looking dates (e.g., 2602.*, 2603.*, 2605.*) consistent with the simulated June 2026 'current' date; verify these resolve to real papers before citation.","'Deployed detection' for insurers is partly marketing: vendors advertise 'deepfake/manipulation detection,' but public evidence shows the robust, in-production capability is mostly duplicate/reused-photo and metadata/anomaly detection, not validated pixel-level AI-edit localization — real capability on small localized edits is largely unproven publicly.","Mendones v. Cushman & Wakefield involved AI-generated/deepfake video and altered images in a housing dispute (detected partly via obvious artifacts), not an insurance claim; it is the closest reported 'deepfake evidence detected in court' case but is not directly an insurance-fraud precedent.","Legal status is in flux: proposed FRE 707 and draft Rule 901(c) were in public comment (comment window cited through Feb 16, 2026) and may change; do not treat them as enacted."]

result.topic: The fraud-domain gap in AI-edit detection for physical DAMAGE photos (auto/property/hotel/receipts), and frontier instruction-editor capability to synthesize localized damage (dents, cracks, scratches, water/mold/fire) on authentic photos. Bottom line: as of mid-2026, AIForge-Doc covers AI-forged DOCUMENTS but no public benchmark/paper covers AI-edited PHYSICAL-DAMAGE photos with per-pixel ground truth; frontier editors can plausibly add localized damage; the convergence of (capability + active fraud + zero damage-domain detection benchmark) is the genuine gap.

key_works.title: AIForge-Doc: A Benchmark for Detecting AI-Forged Tampering in Financial and Form Documents

result.what_detection_runs_today: In practice, insurers run a mix of: (1) commercial/in-house ML claim-screening and 'digital media forensics' (Verisk, plus ~65% third-party + ~50% homegrown AI tools per Verisk 2026), (2) classic image-forensics signals (shadow/lighting inconsistency, repeated-pixel/clone patterns, JPEG/compression and metadata/EXIF analysis), (3) reverse-image/social-media matching (how the LV=/Allianz cracked-bumper case was caught), (4) emerging C2PA/Content-Credentials provenance checks, and (5) general AIGC/inpainting detectors (TruFor, DocTamper, CAT-Net, B-Free, SID detectors) borrowed from the document/forensics literature. Crucially, none of these is trained or benchmarked on AI-edited physical-DAMAGE photos with per-pixel ground truth — the published evidence (AIForge-Doc, TGIF2, 2602.00192) shows these detectors degrade sharply on small localized AI inpaints and over-rely on global artifacts, so confidence on damage-domain edits is essentially unvalidated.
result.the_gap: Confirmed: there is NO public benchmark or paper that detects/localizes small AI edits on PROPERTY/AUTO/HOTEL physical-DAMAGE photos (added dents/cracks/scratches/water-stains/mold/fire) with per-pixel ground truth. The space splits cleanly: (a) the document side is freshly covered by AIForge-Doc (receipts/forms, AI inpainting, pixel masks) — so the receipt half of the fraud domain is addressed; (b) the localized-edit detection methodology exists (DiffSeg30k, LocateEdit-Bench, TGIF2, FragFake all have masks and/or instruction-editor coverage incl. Firefly/Flux/Gemini) — but every one uses generic COCO/OmniEdit object edits with ZERO damage or insurance semantics; (c) the damage-vision side exists (CarDD, with real damage + insurance-grade masks) but only for damage ASSESSMENT, never paired with AI-forgery detection. No work sits at the intersection {authentic damage photo + frontier instruction-edited added-damage + per-pixel forgery mask + detector evaluation}. Additionally, no detection study with per-pixel ground truth evaluates the named frontier instruction editors specifically on the damage-synthesis task; the only damage-domain artifacts are industry white papers (UVeye 2510.19957) and vendor marketing without public data or masks. So beyond AIForge-Doc, the property/auto/damage-photo detection problem is genuinely unaddressed, and CarDD + AIForge-Doc's methodology are the natural building blocks to close it.
fraud_scale_facts: Allianz UK reported a 300% increase in claims where apps were used to distort real images/videos/documents ('shallowfakes') between 2021-22 and 2022-23 (Techdirt/Allianz; FrankonFraud).

Documented case: LV= (Allianz-owned) received a van photo lifted from social media with an AI-added cracked bumper plus a fake repair bill of >£1,000; caught by matching to the original social-media image.

Verisk 2026 State of Insurance Fraud Study (1,000 US consumers + 300 claims pros, Dec 2025–Jan 2026): 98% of insurers say AI editing is fueling more digital fraud; 99% have encountered AI-altered documentation; 76% say altered submissions grew more sophisticated in the past year.
Verisk: insurer detection confidence is 58% for edits to real photos/videos but only 32% for deepfakes; ~65% use third-party AI detection tools, ~50% use homegrown AI.
Verisk consumer side: 36% of consumers would consider digitally altering a claim image/document; 55% of Gen Z are open to it.

Industry/press figures (lower-confidence): AI-edited claim photos reportedly appear in ~23% of fake claims; AI-generated fake receipts rose from ~0% (2024) to ~14% of fraudulent documents by late 2025; an estimate of ~$308.6B annual US AI-generated-image insurance-fraud exposure circulates (vendor-sourced).
UK ABI context: ~45,800 fraudulent motor claims in 2023, motor fraud ~£501M (8% up vs 2022); overall detected fraudulent claims rose to ~£1.1bn in 2024.
result.ethics_data_notes: Defensive framing only — do not publish operational recipes. Frontier editors (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image 'Nano-Banana', gpt-image, Adobe Firefly/Photoshop Generative Fill, Flux.1 Fill) plausibly CAN add localized realistic damage: their documented strengths are exactly fine localized natural-language edits with consistency, and they already power AIForge-Doc (Gemini/Ideogram for receipts) and TGIF2 (Firefly/Flux for object inpainting); a damage-synthesis benchmark should describe capability at a high level and withhold prompt/pipeline specifics. Legal exposure for fraudulent edits is real: property policies' concealment/forfeiture clauses void coverage, and statutes (e.g., NY Penal Law §176.00 et seq., NY Insurance Law §405(a)) criminalize and mandate reporting (Debevoise, Jan 2026). For a defensive dataset: prefer authentic bases with clear licenses (CarDD via request form; COCO; public receipt sets), keep all AI-edited damage strictly within a research/eval sandbox, never attach to real claims, log provenance, and consider C2PA/Content-Credentials labeling of synthetic samples. C2PA is a provenance aid, not a detector — manifests are strippable and absence proves nothing.
result.caveats: Uncertainty flags: (1) arXiv IDs 2602.* / 2603.* (AIForge-Doc, LocateEdit-Bench, TGIF2) are dated early-to-mid 2026 and were read via HTML abstracts/papers, not fully audited — treat scale/AUC numbers as reported-not-verified, and a very recent damage-specific benchmark could exist but be unindexed. (2) The strongest claim ('no damage-photo edit-detection benchmark with per-pixel ground truth') is a negative result from extensive but not exhaustive search; I searched arXiv/web hard and found only document, generic-object, or damage-assessment work, never the intersection. (3) Several fraud-scale figures (23% of fake claims, $308.6B, 14% fake receipts) come from vendor/press sources (TruthScan, ECIKS, FrankonFraud) and should be cited as industry estimates, not peer-reviewed; the Allianz 300%, the LV= case, and the Verisk survey percentages are the most solid. (4) Frontier-editor damage capability is inferred from documented localized-edit strengths and analogous inpainting use (Firefly/Flux in TGIF2, Gemini in AIForge-Doc) plus the real cracked-bumper case — I deliberately did not run or detail any damage-generation pipeline. (5) Property/hotel and water/mold/fire damage have even thinner public data than auto: no mask-annotated authentic base comparable to CarDD was found, so that sub-domain is the most open. (6) Verisk Digital Media Forensics and UVeye capabilities are partly marketing; no independent per-pixel accuracy on damage edits is published.

result.topic: The realistic DEFENDER stack for claim-photo authenticity (EXIF/metadata consistency, PRNU/sensor fingerprint, reverse-image/stock-reuse, perceptual hashing across claims, C2PA/Content Credentials/camera attestation, SynthID, and capture-time provenance insurtech) — and what each catches vs. misses for a small localized AI edit (e.g., an added dent/scratch/water stain) on an otherwise genuine phone JPEG, plus survival of provenance signals under inpainting. Defensive framing: model the real defender to stress-test detectors.

key_works.title: Editing Away the Evidence: Diffusion-Based Image Manipulation and the Failure Modes of Robust Watermarking
key_works.oneline: Systematically tests whether localized/inpainting diffusion edits destroy 'robust' invisible watermarks.
key_works.key_result: Localized diffusion inpainting substantially reduces watermark detectability across SynthID, Tree-Ring, Stable Signature, TrustMark and VINE; re-generating a region effectively strips the per-pixel signal in that region. Directly relevant: an attacker who only edits the damage region locally removes the watermark there while leaving the rest intact, so a single global detector verdict is unreliable.

key_works.title: Authenticated Contradictions from Desynchronized Provenance and Watermarking
key_works.venue: CVPR 2026 Workshop on Authenticity & Provenance in the Age of AI (APAI)
key_works.oneline: Shows C2PA provenance and SynthID-style watermarks can disagree, producing 'authenticated fakes'.
key_works.key_result: Formalizes the 'Integrity Clash': an asset can carry a cryptographically VALID C2PA manifest asserting human authorship while its pixels carry an AI watermark — both checks pass independently. Achieved via 'metadata-washing' through standard editing pipelines (omitting a single permitted assertion field), not crypto breakage. Their cross-layer audit (jointly checking provenance + watermark) reaches 100% classification on 3,500 test images — implying that checking provenance OR watermark alone is exploitable. Authors: Nemecek, He, Cheng, Ayday.

key_works.title: PRNU-based Image Forgery Localization with Deep Multi-scale Fusion
key_works.venue: ACM TOMM (Trans. on Multimedia Computing, Communications & Applications)
key_works.oneline: Deep multi-scale fusion to localize tampered regions from disrupted PRNU sensor noise.
key_works.key_result: PRNU-based methods can in principle localize any tampering type — splicing, copy-move AND inpainting — because re-synthesized regions lose the camera's sensor fingerprint. But the same line of work documents that PRNU is very weak in dark/saturated/textured regions, needs a per-device reference fingerprint (typically ~100-200 flat-field images from the SAME phone), and has high false-positive rates on compressed/cropped images. This is the core 'survives inpainting but rarely deployable for one-off claim JPEGs' result.

key_works.title: On the Influence of Denoising in PRNU based Forgery Detection
key_works.oneline: Classic result that inpainting/denoising erases PRNU in the edited region, enabling detection but also showing fragility.
key_works.key_result: Establishes that any region that is denoised, alpha-matted or inpainted loses its PRNU correlation, which is exactly what makes PRNU a candidate signal against localized AI edits — provided a clean reference fingerprint for that phone exists.

key_works.title: TGIF / TGIF2: Text-Guided Inpainting Forgery Dataset
key_works.oneline: ~75k locally inpainted forgeries (SD2, SDXL, Adobe Firefly) over real COCO photos, with masks.
key_works.key_result: Demonstrates the exact gap a defender must model: classic forgery-localization methods detect splices but FAIL on diffusion-regenerated/inpainted regions, while synthetic-image detectors can flag 'fake' but cannot localize the edited area. Provides real base photos + localized AI edits + ground-truth masks. Code/data on GitHub; source photos CC-BY-4.0 (COCO).

key_works.title: COCO-Inpaint: A Benchmark for Detecting and Localizing Inpainting-Based Image Manipulations
key_works.oneline: Benchmark specifically for inpainting-based localized manipulations over real COCO images.
key_works.key_result: Confirms inpainting localization is a distinct, hard task and that detectors trained on splicing generalize poorly to diffusion inpainting — the precise failure mode a claim-photo defender faces with small added-damage edits.

real_base_datasets.name: AutoSplice
real_base_datasets.contents: 2,273 real + 3,621 manipulated images; text-prompt (DALL-E-2-style) local inpainting over Visual News photos; provided at JPEG QF 75/90/100 to model recompression. Good for testing detector robustness to JPEG.

real_base_datasets.name: CocoGlide
real_base_datasets.contents: 512 photorealistic local inpainting forgeries from COCO 2017 val using the GLIDE diffusion model; small but a standard diffusion-inpainting localization benchmark.

real_base_datasets.name: Classic forgery-localization sets: CASIA v1/v2, Columbia, Coverage, DSO-1, IMD2020
real_base_datasets.contents: CASIA v2 (7,491 authentic / 5,123 forged: splicing, copy-move, removal/inpainting); Columbia (splicing); Coverage (copy-move); DSO-1 (spliced + masks); IMD2020 ('in-the-wild' real manipulations from the internet with manual masks). These are the legacy baselines a defender's localizer is usually trained/evaluated on — and which generalize poorly to modern diffusion inpainting.

real_base_datasets.name: 'Zooming In on Fakes' — Localized AI-Generated Image dataset
real_base_datasets.contents: Recent dataset purpose-built for detecting SMALL localized AI edits on real photos (vs. fully synthetic), using a forgery-amplification approach. Closest in spirit to the claim-photo threat model.

result.what_detection_runs_today: In production claim pipelines the realistic defender stack is layered and leans heavily on the CHEAP, ROBUST layers rather than a pixel-perfect inpainting localizer: (1) Reuse/duplicate detection — perceptual hashing + visual embeddings against the carrier's own archive and cross-carrier databases (Verisk ClaimSearch Image Matching, VAARHAFT cross-insurance duplicate check) plus reverse-image search (TinEye/Yandex/Google) for stock/web reuse; this is the highest-yield, most reliable layer. (2) Metadata/EXIF consistency — checking capture timestamp, timezone, geotag and device against the claim story, and flagging missing/stripped metadata or screenshots (insurers therefore demand ORIGINAL files, not screenshots). (3) Classic pixel forensics — Error Level Analysis and noise/clone forensics with heatmaps; Zurich's fraud team explicitly credits metadata anomalies + ELA for catching fake car images. (4) A newer GenAI/deepfake image classifier (Verisk deepfake module, VAARHAFT, TruthScan) giving a probabilistic 'manipulated?' score. (5) Entity/network analytics (Quantexa at Zurich) connecting claims/people. Capture-time provenance (Truepic Lens, Serelay; C2PA) is the strongest single control but is only present where the insurer forces in-app capture — it is adopted for virtual inspections but is NOT yet the default for inbound claimant photos. SynthID/watermark detection plays essentially no role in claim photos because the genuine base image is unwatermarked and only the edit might (or might not) carry a watermark.
result.the_gap: No single signal reliably catches a SMALL localized AI edit (added dent/scratch/water stain) on an otherwise genuine, freshly-captured phone JPEG — which is exactly the threat the project should stress-test. Reuse/reverse-image/perceptual-hash layers see nothing because the photo is genuinely new and unique. Metadata/EXIF is clean because the base capture is real and the editing app can preserve/regenerate plausible EXIF (and many insurers only check for MISSING/inconsistent metadata, not subtle edits). PRNU — the one passive signal that genuinely survives and localizes inpainting (the edited region loses the sensor fingerprint) — is rarely usable in practice: it needs ~100-200 reference images from the SAME phone to estimate the fingerprint, fails in dark/saturated/textured regions (where damage often is), and degrades badly under social-media recompression/cropping. C2PA proves nothing for an unsigned consumer JPEG (no manifest to break), can be stripped silently by messaging/upload re-encoding, and is vulnerable to re-signing / 'metadata-washing' that yields 'authenticated fakes' (Integrity Clash). SynthID/robust watermarks are largely absent on the base photo and, per 'Editing Away the Evidence,' localized diffusion inpainting strips the watermark precisely in the edited region while leaving the rest detectable — so a global verdict misleads. GenAI image classifiers and forgery localizers trained on splicing/older GANs generalize poorly to modern diffusion inpainting (TGIF, COCO-Inpaint) and small edits sit below their thresholds. Net: the genuinely hard, under-defended case is the localized diffusion inpaint on a real phone capture, and the only durable defenses are (a) capture-time provenance enforced at intake (Truepic/Serelay) and (b) PRNU when the actual phone is available — neither of which most inbound claims satisfy.
fraud_scale_facts: Allianz UK: incidents using apps to distort real images/videos/documents rose ~300% between 2021-22 and 2022-23 ('shallowfakes' — edits made with phone apps/Photoshop to add damage or alter details), warning it has 'all the signs of becoming the latest big scam' (May 2024).

UK insurers reported a rise in manipulated car-damage images in May 2024 — fraudsters adding dents/scratches and fake registration plates to photos that pass simple checks (Express & Star, PetaPixel, inkl).

Zurich: real-time fraud detection (Quantexa partnership) detected the equivalent of ~£260,000 of bogus claims every day in 2024; fraud team credits catching fake car images via metadata anomalies + Error Level Analysis.

Verisk Digital Media Forensics example: a staged Segway-accident scheme was uncovered when the same damage photos were matched across SIX different carriers within a month (image traced to a Reddit post).
Synthetic-voice fraud at insurers rose 475% in 2024, contributing to a ~19% YoY rise in overall insurance fraud attempts (note: voice, not image).

Deepfake fraud attempts across financial services rose ~2,100% over three years and deepfakes were ~6.5% of all fraud attacks; average deepfake loss ~US$600k/incident (Signicat/Regula — broad FS, not image-specific).

Industry surveys: only ~22% of organizations have implemented measures specifically against AI-driven fraud; insurers cited as ~20x more exposed than banks due to reliance on documents/images/voice in claims.
result.ethics_data_notes: Defensive use only. All recommended datasets are public, research-released, and built on permissively-licensed real photos: TGIF/TGIF2, CocoGlide and COCO-Inpaint derive from MS-COCO (CC-BY-4.0); AutoSplice derives from Visual News; classic sets (CASIA/Columbia/Coverage/DSO-1/IMD2020) are standard public forensics benchmarks. These supply REAL base photos + localized AI/inpainting edits + ground-truth masks, so a stress-test of detectors needs no creation of new fraudulent claim material. For PRNU experiments, use public source-camera datasets (e.g., Dresden Image Database, VISION) for reference fingerprints rather than real claimants' devices. Do NOT scrape or reuse real insurance claim photos (PII: plates, faces, addresses, geolocation) — use synthetic/staged damage or the public datasets above. Keep the work to measuring detector failure rates and provenance-signal survival; do not publish per-tool evasion procedures. C2PA/Content Credentials, Truepic/Serelay, SynthID and Verisk verdicts should be treated as black-box defenders to evaluate, with results reported as catch/miss rates, not as bypass instructions.
result.caveats: ["Several of the most on-point sources are 2026 arXiv PREPRINTS (2603.12949 'Editing Away the Evidence'; 2603.02378 APAI workshop) — not yet peer-reviewed/widely replicated; treat their headline numbers (e.g., 100% cross-layer audit accuracy) as indicative, not settled. The arXiv IDs are unusually recent and should be re-verified.","Vendor capability claims (Verisk deepfake module, VAARHAFT '48h to new generators', Truepic, TruthScan accuracy figures) are largely marketing; independent benchmark evidence on SUBTLE localized inpainting (vs. fully synthetic images) is thin. The deepfake/GenAI classifiers' real catch rate on small edits is the biggest uncertainty.","There is NO authoritative public statistic for the prevalence or $ loss of LOCALIZED-AI-edited claim photos specifically; the deetech 2026 report explicitly states 'no single authoritative source tracks deepfake fraud in insurance.' The 300% 'shallowfake' figure covers app-based edits broadly (incl. non-AI Photoshop), and many cited deepfake stats are VOICE/identity fraud, not damage-photo edits — do not over-generalize them to image fraud.","PRNU's 'survives inpainting' property is real in the lab but its practical usability for one-off claim JPEGs (reference-fingerprint requirement, textured/dark-region failure, recompression sensitivity) means it is best modeled as an 'only-if-phone-available' control, not a default defender.","C2PA adoption in inbound claimant photos is still low; statements that insurers 'use C2PA' mostly refer to insurer-controlled in-app capture (Truepic/Serelay virtual inspections), not consumer phones — verify per-carrier before assuming it is in the live defender stack.","Some retrieved fraud statistics come from vendor blogs (TruthScan, deetech, VAARHAFT) that have a commercial interest; cross-check against primary insurer statements (Allianz, Zurich) where possible."]

synth.verified_core_claims: CONFIRMED (high confidence, cross-checked via arXiv abs/HTML + Semantic Scholar CorpusIds/DOIs + project pages): (1) INP-X = arXiv:2602.00192 — all four headline collapse pairs verbatim-confirmed: Hive 91.4->54.8, Sightengine 92.6->55.0, Corvi2023 94.2->55.4, SPAI 66.1->54.2; 90K benchmark over CelebA-HQ/CityScapes/OpenImages/SUN-RGBD; mechanism = VAE-induced global spectral shift. (2) LocalizedDeepfakes = arXiv:2512.16688 — exists with stated title/authors (Pandolfini et al., Univ. Bologna); the qualitative size-dependence claims CONFIRMED (<5% mask ~chance; recovery >20%; DINOv3 comparable at ~65% mask, DINOv2 >80%); three backbones (ResNet-50 CLIP/DINOv2/DINOv3) and datasets (BR-Gen/TGIF/TGIF2) confirmed. (3) DiQuID/SAGI-D = arXiv:2502.06593 — exists; 95,839 inpainted from 78,684 originals (MS-COCO/RAISE-RAW/OpenImages); UGDA pipeline; SP vs FR split; human accuracy 74%->35%; in-domain +37.4% / OOD +26.1% IoU all confirmed. (4) AIForge-Doc = arXiv:2602.20569 — exists; median tampered area 0.92% (claim said ~1%); DocTamper AUC 0.98->0.563, TruFor 0.751, GPT-4o 0.509; 4,061 forged from CORD/WildReceipt/SROIE/XFUND via Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (89.6%) + Ideogram v2 (10.4%) all confirmed. (5) The four-paper group all REAL: COCO-Inpaint 2504.18361 (six inpainters incl. Flux.1-Fill/BrushNet/PowerPaint; cross-model Pixel-F1 86.4->24.6 verbatim in v2 Table 3), TGIF 2407.11566 (WIFS 2024), DiffSeg30k 2511.19111 (30k COCO, 8 editors, multi-turn), TGIF2 2603.28613 (real Springer/EURASIP DOI 10.1186/s13635-026-00235-9). Cross-cutting confirmed fact: NONE of the verified papers is fraud-domain — all use faces/scenes/COCO/RAISE or generic documents; none does a parametric edit-size x blending sweep, tests a broad commercial-API panel, or runs a laundering/re-compression robustness sweep (TGIF2 only studies generative-SR laundering). The defensive small-localized-edit-on-authentic-photo framing is the project's, not any single paper's stated motivation.
